raw_graphql_pull_request.body:
## Overview

Part of #63818 (RFC: pluggable PP transport), Phase 1. Adds `--pp-group-cls`, which lets a plugin supply the `GroupCoordinator` of the pipeline-parallel group, and routes the V2 model runner's sampled-token broadcast through that group (`sibling_broadcast`), so a plugin can carry all PP traffic over its own transport.

## Claims

- `ParallelConfig.pp_group_cls` / `--pp-group-cls <qualname>`: `initialize_model_parallel` constructs the PP group with this `GroupCoordinator` subclass (same arguments); TP/DP/EP/PCP/DCP groups are unchanged. Default `""` keeps `GroupCoordinator`; a name that is not a subclass fails at startup. Same pattern as `--worker-cls`.
- `GroupCoordinator.sibling_broadcast(tensor, src, group)`: `PPHandler` (MRV2) now issues its sampled-token / draft broadcasts through it instead of calling `torch.distributed.broadcast` directly. The default implementation is that same call, so there is no behaviour change; a PP group class overrides it together with `make_sibling_device_group`.
- With these two, an out-of-tree PP group (here: UCX via connex-rs) serves Llama-3-8B with PP=2 and PP=4 on vLLM main with the default V2 model runner, greedy outputs pass a teacher-forced check, and latency/throughput are within a few percent of NCCL (numbers below).

## Validation

Unit tests (CPU, gloo, world size 1):

```
pytest tests/distributed/test_pp_group_cls.py -v       # 4 passed
pre-commit run --files <changed files>                  # ruff, mypy, typos, docs hooks: pass
```

`test_pp_handler_broadcasts_through_pp_group` checks that `PPHandler.broadcast` goes through the PP group's `sibling_broadcast`; `test_sibling_broadcast_default_uses_torch_distributed` checks the default.

End to end, with a plugin PP group that moves the hidden states and the sampled tokens over UCX (connex-rs, one-sided RDMA reads, GPUDirect): `vllm serve <Llama-3-8B> -pp N --pp-group-cls connex.adapters.vllm.pp.group.ConnexPPGroup --worker-cls connex.adapters.vllm.pp.worker.ConnexPPWorker` vs. the same command without the flags (NCCL). NVIDIA A40 GPUs (PCIe, no NVLink), ConnectX 100 Gb InfiniBand; `vllm bench serve --dataset-name random --random-input-len 512 --random-output-len 128 --ignore-eos`, `--max-concurrency` C, 8·C prompts (≥ 32), one run per cell; median TPOT (ms) / output tok/s:

| setup | C=1 NCCL | C=1 plugin | C=8 NCCL | C=8 plugin | C=32 NCCL | C=32 plugin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PP=2, one host | 28.24 / 34.1 | 29.04 / 33.8 | 32.99 / 218.6 | 33.01 / 232.9 | 41.85 / 717.3 | 40.38 / 736.9 |
| PP=4, one host | 28.32 / 34.0 | 29.55 / 33.2 | 31.65 / 223.5 | 32.94 / 232.6 | 39.04 / 754.0 | 40.54 / 739.1 |
| PP=2 x TP=2, one host | 15.53 / 60.3 | 16.09 / 60.3 | 17.66 / 378.6 | 17.61 / 423.7 | 22.40 / 1263.9 | 22.47 / 1254.6 |
| PP=2, two hosts (`--nnodes 2`) | 28.27 / 34.1 | 28.98 / 33.3 | 33.23 / 218.9 | 33.35 / 218.2 | 41.06 / 728.4 | 40.53 / 729.1 |

Correctness: 16 greedy requests × 200 tokens per setup, every generated token re-scored by teacher forcing on a non-PP (TP=1) vLLM instance: 0 of 3,200 generated tokens more than 0.5 nats below the argmax in every setup, with NCCL and with the plugin (worst gap 0.125 nats, the same as non-PP vs non-PP).

Per-hop latency of the same API (`benchmarks/pp_upstream/bench_p2p.py` in the plugin repo: two ranks ping-pong `isend_tensor_dict`/`irecv_tensor_dict` of `{hidden_states, residual}`, bf16, hidden 4096, one way = round trip / 2, median of 200, synchronized per iteration):

| tokens (bytes) | one host: NCCL | one host: plugin | two hosts: NCCL | two hosts: plugin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (16 KB) | 412 µs | 650 µs | 467 µs (p99 2,574) | 697 µs (p99 759) |
| 64 (1 MB) | 403 µs | 823 µs | 516 µs | 786 µs |
| 512 (8 MB) | 518 µs | 1,469 µs | 1,660 µs | 1,834 µs |
| 2048 (32 MB) | 1,543 µs | 4,474 µs | 5,994 µs | 5,652 µs |

The plugin is slower per hop on one host (its GPU-to-GPU path is RDMA loopback through the NIC, NCCL uses PCIe P2P) and for small messages (Python on the path); end to end this mostly does not show because its receive does not block the CPU (see Details). These per-hop numbers are not a property of this PR, only context for the RFC.

The NCCL rows are vLLM main unchanged (the flag is not set); NCCL path numbers are not affected by this PR (the default `sibling_broadcast` is the old call).

## Details

- Why a class name and not a registry: it mirrors `--worker-cls` / `--worker-extension-cls`; plugins only need to be importable. If #50853 lands a `PPTransport` owner, this flag can select that class instead.
- Why `sibling_broadcast` is needed: with MRV2, PP traffic is not only `isend/irecv_tensor_dict`; the last rank broadcasts sampled tokens on a sibling NCCL communicator. Without the hook a plugin that replaces the transport still needs NCCL for this, which defeats the purpose (e.g. stages that are not in one NCCL communicator).
- The plugin used above, for reference only (not part of this PR): https://github.com/HeterInfra/connex, `connex/adapters/vllm/pp`. Its receive path makes the CUDA stream wait for a host flag (`cuStreamWaitValue32`), which keeps the CPU of the receiving stage off the critical path like a NCCL receive.
- Not a duplicate: open PRs touching PP communication change the in-tree transport or the MRV2 PP schedule; none makes the PP group replaceable (searched `#63818`, "pp-group-cls", "pipeline parallel GroupCoordinator plugin").
- Follow-ups in the RFC: running each stage as its own instance (`--pipeline-stage-rank`, separate PR stacked on this one) and recomputing requests whose KV was lost on a replaced stage (separate PR).

Developed with AI coding assistance; all changes were reviewed and tested by the author.

---

- [x] **Design Fit:** Minimizes impact on core components, reuses existing functionality, and justifies added complexity.

</details>

🚀

Update on the numbers in the description (no code change in this PR).

The plugin now moves same-host stage-to-stage traffic over CUDA IPC with `cuStreamWaitValue32` / `cuStreamWriteValue32` on shared pinned flags, so nothing on the data path runs in Python, as with NCCL. Cross-host hops stay RDMA. Re-measured on 4x A40 (PCIe), Llama-3-8B, 3 runs per cell (mean ± std), median TPOT ms:

| | C=1 NCCL | C=1 plugin | C=8 NCCL | C=8 plugin | C=32 NCCL | C=32 plugin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PP=2 | 28.24 ±0.00 | 28.23 ±0.01 | 33.03 ±0.43 | 32.94 ±0.07 | 41.55 ±1.24 | 40.65 ±1.35 |
| PP=4 | 28.33 ±0.00 | 28.35 ±0.00 | 32.77 ±1.90 | 31.93 ±1.60 | 40.21 ±1.10 | 40.20 ±0.19 |
| PP=2 x TP=2 | 15.53 ±0.00 | 15.51 ±0.01 | 17.62 ±0.17 | 17.76 ±0.09 | 22.87 ±0.10 | 23.20 ±0.38 |

Within run-to-run noise in every cell (the single runs in the description, over RDMA loopback, were 2-4% slower at C=1). Two hosts (RDMA, 3 runs): C=1 28.28 vs 28.94 ms, p99 TPOT 28.28 vs 29.08 ms; C=32 41.00 vs 41.87 ms.

Per hop, same `isend/irecv_tensor_dict` calls, one host, 3 runs: 32 MB 1.54 ±0.00 ms (NCCL) vs 0.80 ±0.04 ms (plugin); 16 KB 0.41 ±0.01 vs 0.52 ±0.12 ms (the plugin's small-message latency is noisy, Python on the control path).

One design note relevant to this API: a stream wait that only a Python thread of the same process can release deadlocks against CUDA calls that hold the GIL and synchronize the device (a first Triton kernel load does). The plugin avoids it on one host by having the sender's GPU release the receiver's waits. Across hosts the waits are still released by a Python thread, so the risk remains there outside warmup (where it waits on the CPU instead).

### 🟡 Changes recommended The new broadcast-delegation test fails on XPU because its stream fake lacks the required `synchronize()` method.
1 open issue - [Add synchronize() to fake main stream](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/63897#discussion_r4384297383) · New
What changed in this PR Implements Phase 1 of the pluggable pipeline-parallel transport RFC, allowing plugins to replace PP coordination while preserving the default transport. **Changes:** - Adds `--pp-group-cls` and validates the configured `GroupCoordinator` subclass. - Routes Model Runner V2 sampled-token and draft broadcasts through an overridable PP hook. - Adds focused tests and documents class-based plugin selection. | File | Description | | ---- | ----------- | | `vllm/​v1/​worker/​gpu/​pp_utils.py` | Delegates broadcasts to the PP coordinator. | | `vllm/​engine/​arg_utils.py` | Wires the new CLI option into configuration. | | `vllm/​distributed/​parallel_state.py` | Resolves the PP subclass and adds the broadcast hook. | | `vllm/​config/​parallel.py` | Defines the PP class setting and excludes it from hashing. | | `tests/​distributed/​test_pp_group_cls.py` | Tests class selection, validation, and broadcast delegation. | | `docs/​design/​plugin_system.md` | Documents PP coordinator customization. |
Review effort: Balanced

On XPU, `PPHandler.broadcast()` calls `self.main_stream.synchronize()` before broadcasting (`pp_utils.py:262–263`). This test assigns `_NullStream` to `main_stream`, but the fake only implements `wait_stream`, so the test raises `AttributeError` before reaching its assertions on that supported platform. Add a no-op `synchronize()` method to the fake.

+

+    monkeypatch.setattr(pp_utils.torch.cuda, "stream", lambda s: contextlib.nullcontext())
+    monkeypatch.setattr(torch.Tensor, "record_stream", lambda self, stream: None)
+    handler = pp_utils.PPHandler(max_num_reqs=4, num_speculative_steps=0, device="cpu")

+
+    batch = SimpleNamespace(
+        num_computed_tokens_np=np.array([4, 4]),
+        prefill_len_np=np.array([4, 4]),
+        num_scheduled_tokens=np.array([1, 1]),
+        max_seq_len_np=None,
+        is_prefilling_np=np.array([False, False]),

+    assert calls == [((2, 1), 1, "sibling"), ((2, 2), 1, "sibling")]
+
+
+class _NullStream:
+    def wait_stream(self, stream):
+        pass

| PP=2, two hosts (`--nnodes 2`) | 28.27 / 34.1 | 28.98 / 33.3 | 33.23 / 218.9 | 33.35 / 218.2 | 41.06 / 728.4 | 40.53 / 729.1 |

Correctness: 16 greedy requests × 200 tokens per setup, every generated token re-scored by teacher forcing on a non-PP (TP=1) vLLM instance: 0 of 3,200 generated tokens more than 0.5 nats below the argmax in every setup, with NCCL and with the plugin (worst gap 0.125 nats, the same as non-PP vs non-PP).

Per-hop latency of the same API (`benchmarks/pp_upstream/bench_p2p.py` in the plugin repo: two ranks ping-pong `isend_tensor_dict`/`irecv_tensor_dict` of `{hidden_states, residual}`, bf16, hidden 4096, one way = round trip / 2, median of 200, synchronized per iteration):

| tokens (bytes) | one host: NCCL | one host: plugin | two hosts: NCCL | two hosts: plugin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (16 KB) | 412 µs | 650 µs | 467 µs (p99 2,574) | 697 µs (p99 759) |
| 64 (1 MB) | 403 µs | 823 µs | 516 µs | 786 µs |
| 512 (8 MB) | 518 µs | 1,469 µs | 1,660 µs | 1,834 µs |
| 2048 (32 MB) | 1,543 µs | 4,474 µs | 5,994 µs | 5,652 µs |

The plugin is slower per hop on one host (its GPU-to-GPU path is RDMA loopback through the NIC, NCCL uses PCIe P2P) and for small messages (Python on the path); end to end this mostly does not show because its receive does not block the CPU (see Details). These per-hop numbers are not a property of this PR, only context for the RFC.

The NCCL rows are vLLM main unchanged (the flag is not set); NCCL path numbers are not affected by this PR (the default `sibling_broadcast` is the old call).

## Details

- Why a class name and not a registry: it mirrors `--worker-cls` / `--worker-extension-cls`; plugins only need to be importable. If #50853 lands a `PPTransport` owner, this flag can select that class instead.
- Why `sibling_broadcast` is needed: with MRV2, PP traffic is not only `isend/irecv_tensor_dict`; the last rank broadcasts sampled tokens on a sibling NCCL communicator. Without the hook a plugin that replaces the transport still needs NCCL for this, which defeats the purpose (e.g. stages that are not in one NCCL communicator).
- The plugin used above, for reference only (not part of this PR): https://github.com/HeterInfra/connex, `connex/adapters/vllm/pp`. Its receive path makes the CUDA stream wait for a host flag (`cuStreamWaitValue32`), which keeps the CPU of the receiving stage off the critical path like a NCCL receive.
- Not a duplicate: open PRs touching PP communication change the in-tree transport or the MRV2 PP schedule; none makes the PP group replaceable (searched `#63818`, "pp-group-cls", "pipeline parallel GroupCoordinator plugin").
- Follow-ups in the RFC: running each stage as its own instance (`--pipeline-stage-rank`, separate PR stacked on this one) and recomputing requests whose KV was lost on a replaced stage (separate PR).

Developed with AI coding assistance; all changes were reviewed and tested by the author.

+                local_rank=0,

+                cleanup_dist_env_and_memory()

+        with contextlib.suppress(OSError):
+            os.unlink(path)
+

+        pp_group.sibling_broadcast(tensor, src=pp_group.last_rank, group=sibling)
+        assert tensor.tolist() == [0, 1, 2, 3]
+
+
+def test_pp_handler_broadcasts_through_pp_group(monkeypatch):
+    """The V2 runner's sampled-token broadcast goes through the PP group, so
+    a `pp_group_cls` can carry it over its own transport."""
+    from vllm.v1.worker.gpu import pp_utils
+
+    calls = []
+
+    class FakePPGroup:
+        is_last_rank = True
+        last_rank = 1
+        world_size = 2
+
+        def make_sibling_device_group(self, group_desc=None):
+            return "sibling"
+
+        def sibling_broadcast(self, tensor, src, group):
+            calls.append((tuple(tensor.shape), src, group))
+
+    monkeypatch.setattr(pp_utils, "get_pp_group", FakePPGroup)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(pp_utils.torch.cuda, "current_stream", lambda device: None)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(pp_utils.torch.cuda, "Stream", lambda device: None)
+    monkeypatch.setattr(
+        pp_utils.torch.cuda, "stream", lambda s: contextlib.nullcontext()
+    )
+    monkeypatch.setattr(torch.Tensor, "record_stream", lambda self, stream: None)
+    handler = pp_utils.PPHandler(max_num_reqs=4, num_speculative_steps=0, device="cpu")
+    handler.main_stream = handler.broadcast_stream = _NullStream()
+
+    batch = SimpleNamespace(
+        num_computed_tokens_np=np.array([4, 4]),
+        prefill_len_np=np.array([4, 4]),
+        num_scheduled_tokens=np.array([1, 1]),
+        max_seq_len_np=None,
+        is_prefilling_np=np.array([False, False]),
+        num_draft_tokens=0,
+    )
+    sampled = torch.zeros(2, 1, dtype=torch.int64)
+    handler.broadcast(

+        torch.zeros(2, dtype=torch.int32),

+

+    def wait_stream(self, stream):
+        pass
+

+        # PPHandler.broadcast() synchronizes the main stream on XPU.
+        pass

This test assigns `_NullStream` to `main_stream`, but the fake only implements `wait_stream`, so the test raises `AttributeError` before reaching its assertions on that supported platform. Update on the numbers in the description (no code change in this PR).

The plugin now moves same-host stage-to-stage traffic over CUDA IPC with `cuStreamWaitValue32` / `cuStreamWriteValue32` on shared pinned flags, so nothing on the data path runs in Python, as with NCCL. Cross-host hops stay RDMA. Re-measured on 4x A40 (PCIe), Llama-3-8B, 3 runs per cell (mean ± std), median TPOT ms:

| | C=1 NCCL | C=1 plugin | C=8 NCCL | C=8 plugin | C=32 NCCL | C=32 plugin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PP=2 | 28.24 ±0.00 | 28.23 ±0.01 | 33.03 ±0.43 | 32.94 ±0.07 | 41.55 ±1.24 | 40.65 ±1.35 |
| PP=4 | 28.33 ±0.00 | 28.35 ±0.00 | 32.77 ±1.90 | 31.93 ±1.60 | 40.21 ±1.10 | 40.20 ±0.19 |
| PP=2 x TP=2 | 15.53 ±0.00 | 15.51 ±0.01 | 17.62 ±0.17 | 17.76 ±0.09 | 22.87 ±0.10 | 23.20 ±0.38 |

Within run-to-run noise in every cell (the single runs in the description, over RDMA loopback, were 2-4% slower at C=1). Two hosts (RDMA, 3 runs): C=1 28.28 vs 28.94 ms, p99 TPOT 28.28 vs 29.08 ms; C=32 41.00 vs 41.87 ms.

Per hop, same `isend/irecv_tensor_dict` calls, one host, 3 runs: 32 MB 1.54 ±0.00 ms (NCCL) vs 0.80 ±0.04 ms (plugin); 16 KB 0.41 ±0.01 vs 0.52 ±0.12 ms (the plugin's small-message latency is noisy, Python on the control path).

One design note relevant to this API: a stream wait that only a Python thread of the same process can release deadlocks against CUDA calls that hold the GIL and synchronize the device (a first Triton kernel load does). The plugin avoids it on one host by having the sender's GPU release the receiver's waits. Across hosts the waits are still released by a Python thread, so the risk remains there outside warmup (where it waits on the CPU instead).
